facts.text: A civil action may be dismissed for want of prosecution if no step has been taken that materially advances the action for five years or more, under Rule 327(1)(b) of the Rules of Court.
facts.why_it_matters: This rule mandates automatic dismissal if there is no material progress in the action for five years, regardless of prejudice or justification for the delay. This is a strict procedural rule that prioritizes efficiency over the merits of the case.
facts.if_changed: If the rule were discretionary, the court would have more flexibility to consider the reasons for delay, including strategic decisions like waiting for class action certification.

facts.text: The court may dismiss an action for want of prosecution if there has been inordinate and inexcusable delay, which is presumed to cause significant prejudice.
facts.why_it_matters: This creates a rebuttable presumption that delay causes prejudice, which can be used to justify dismissal even if the delay was strategic. The burden is on the plaintiff to show that the delay was justified.
facts.if_changed: If the court were required to prove actual prejudice, the plaintiff might have a better chance of avoiding dismissal, even if the delay was strategic.

facts.text: Strategic delay, such as waiting for class action certification, may not be a valid justification for avoiding dismissal under Rule 327(1)(b).
facts.why_it_matters: The evidence suggests that the court does not consider the reason for delay when applying the five-year rule. Strategic decisions to delay are treated the same as other forms of inaction.
facts.if_changed: If strategic delay were recognized as a valid justification, the plaintiff might be able to avoid dismissal by showing that the delay was necessary for procedural or tactical reasons.

facts.text: The court may dismiss an action for want of prosecution even if the delay was not caused by the plaintiff.
facts.why_it_matters: This is a key point in cases where the delay was caused by the defendant or third parties. The rule does not require the plaintiff to be at fault for the delay.
facts.if_changed: If the rule required the plaintiff to be at fault for the delay, then strategic decisions by the plaintiff to delay might be more easily justified.

facts.text: The court may consider whether the delay was inexcusable and whether it caused prejudice to the other party.
facts.why_it_matters: While the five-year rule is mandatory, the court may still consider the impact of the delay on the other party. This is relevant in cases where the delay was strategic but did not cause significant prejudice.
facts.if_changed: If the court were required to find actual prejudice, then strategic delays that did not harm the other party might not lead to dismissal.

facts.text: The court may dismiss an action for want of prosecution even if the plaintiff has taken some steps to advance the case, but not enough to meet the 'materially advances' standard.
facts.why_it_matters: This is a high bar for the plaintiff. Even if the plaintiff has taken some steps, they must show that those steps significantly advanced the case.
facts.if_changed: If the standard were lower, the plaintiff might have a better chance of avoiding dismissal, even if the delay was strategic.
